Fixed-provenance reversed delivery also swaps explicit-title and filename-fallback authorship to prove both presence/removal winner directions.

entries.title: Provider-delivered nested pages converge even when receiver parent directories do not yet exist
entries.notes: Fail-before: an honest offline device created notes/provider-created/deep/physical-source.md and published it through ordinary external-file admission. After complete provider delivery, receiver crash/restart, and duplicate redelivery, a receiver lacking only provider-created/deep remained permanently blocked with authenticated expected-path authority missing and never projected the page. Pre-creating only that parent chain made the exact scenario converge. Projection input capture now reports a stably missing ancestor as semantic absence while ordinary files, symlinks/reparse points, special entries, permission failures, and traversal races remain errors. Present publication reaches the retained-capability recursive writer; a retry resumes after a synced partial chain, while a proven nested tombstone completes without creating parents. The original duplicate-delivery/restart scenario now drains provider work and produces parser-visible receiver bytes.

entries.title: Windows projection and SQLite lease safety use stable public held-handle filesystem APIs
entries.notes: Fail-before: hosted Windows run 30507282266 at exact candidate 7792d3062936e28c2da2089693fd9f644e43305e failed to compile because projection_file_link_count used unstable std::os::windows::fs::MetadataExt::number_of_links and entry_file_identity resolved file_attributes on cap_std metadata to a private implementation method. Projection link count now comes from GetFileInformationByHandle on the already-held file handle, and capability metadata attributes use explicit public cap_fs_ext::OsMetadataExt dispatch. Existing no-follow opens, pre-open and held-handle reparse checks, single-link refusal, identity validation, and error classification remain unchanged.

entries.title: Managed storage reopens promptly after an unclean shutdown even when its reconstructible resume accelerator is unavailable
entries.notes: Negative follow-up on 2026-08-05 revoked the deployed-state evidence: v0.6.90 again took roughly 60 seconds to recover a managed graph. Current master still passes the original permitted 1,045-file anonymized fresh-copy receipt (ordinary pending-save crash takeover 0.19 seconds; forced resume-accelerator removal 6.85 seconds), so the missing regression fixture is accumulated or failed-transaction state rather than the original fresh activation alone. Historical fail-before on 92edd261 took 30.9 seconds locally and about 58 seconds on the user's slower machine; fe5dfb7f reconstructed the immutable bootstrap once and reduced that exact case to 2.36 seconds. entries.title: A missing remembered graph path cannot prevent startup and leaves the graph chooser usable
entries.notes: GH #250 failed on v0.6.5 because the missing remembered graph was opened synchronously from native setup and panicked before a usable app appeared. The later abf7af83 startup refactor co-fixed it by deferring graph loading to the visible frontend. The semantic regression proves the failed remembered-root load completes startup and exposes an enabled Open an existing graph action; the native structural neighbor proves setup no longer invokes graph loading. No filesystem path is created or mutated by this frontend recovery path.

entries.title: Inactive bootstrap and live-runtime contention honor Windows filesystem semantics
entries.notes: Fail-before: exact serial hosted Windows runs 30986757145 and 30992636156 reached live-runtime bootstrap capture and failed with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED. Instrumented run 30994134161 on cf2ca70f localized the first failure to flush_bootstrap_source_prefix. On non-Linux targets that durability pass recursively opened each regular capture artifact with File::open (GENERIC_READ on Windows) and then called sync_all (FlushFileBuffers on Windows); FlushFileBuffers requires write access and therefore returned ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED on the valid read-only handle. Fixed by e04469c3 using the established shadow-projection and migration-backup pattern: request write access only for the Windows regular-file flush handle, preserve read-only access elsewhere, and propagate every open or flush error. Hosted pass-after run 30995033385 proved capture now completes, then exposed the same legacy portability defect in prepare_inactive_bootstrap_import: its non-Linux preparation-tree flush also used read-only File::open handles for file FlushFileBuffers, while its recursive, post-rename, and retry directory barriers bypassed Tine's explicit Windows directory-sync contract. Fixed by 87a41863: preparation file barriers use Windows write access, and every preparation directory barrier now uses tine-storage ValidatedDirectorySync, which validates a real non-reparse retained capability and explicitly records Windows directory-entry crash durability as unsupported after validation. No PermissionDenied or other open/flush error is ignored. Hosted run 30995785773 proved both production stages pass, then exposed a test-oracle defect: authoritative_world used the generic whole-tree snapshot and filtered .tine-runtime and engine-scratch-v2 only after reading them. The helper process intentionally holds the archive-rooted lease, so Windows correctly rejected reading the locked lease with ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION while Unix advisory locking had hidden the mistake. Fixed test-only by 8cd3e322 with a path-filtered walker that prunes non-authoritative namespaces before opening contents while continuing to hash every selected durable file. The same caller audit moved volatile SQLite -shm exclusion, lease-namespace exclusion, and immutable batches/objects selection before reads; generic whole-tree snapshots remain unchanged. Hosted run 30996661360 proved the archive-lease pruning worked, then exposed the device-local enrollment lease at sparse-storage/v2/local/<graph>/enrollment/lease: its stable file identity, not its locked empty bytes, is authority and is already bound into every authenticated enrollment record and revalidated separately. Fixed test-only by d9f78a09 by excluding that exact six-component lease path before reads while continuing to hash its authoritative enrollment head and all other durable siblings; snapshot read panics now include root and relative path. A guarded-reader regression proves neither locked lease reaches the reader and authoritative siblings are still hashed. Hosted run 30997515786 then reached the intended same-profile contention operation, but fs2's Windows LockFileEx failure surfaced ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION (33) with ErrorKind::Uncategorized and enrollment mapped it to generic I/O. Fixed by 0c942015 with one shared narrow nonblocking-lock classifier: WouldBlock everywhere plus exact Windows ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION. Enrollment, SQLite, and projection mutation leases retain their preexisting explicit PermissionDenied policy; packed-Patricia and object-store transition locks do not gain it. ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION (32) remains an open/share-mode error, not contention, because fs2 calls LockFileEx only after the file is open. The breadth audit found direct Windows LockFileEx implementations in local-journal, scratch, and simulator already classify exactly code 33; blocking object-store locks need no nonblocking mapping. Focused helpers directly exercise durability and lock contracts; the unchanged full live-runtime witness, capture family, preparation seal/retry, enrollment, SQLite, packed-Patricia, and object-store serialization tests cover the surrounding fail-closed protocol. Linux and Android use syncfs for both prefixes and never enter the recursive per-file FlushFileBuffers paths.

entries.title: An unsaved edit is not conflicted by a change notification that carries no per-page divergence

tests: src/App.test.tsx::does not conflict a dirty page when the admitted epoch left it unchanged
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page when the stored revision genuinely moved
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page whose file was deleted under it
src/App.test.tsx::leaves an in-flight save alone — its own base_rev guard is the authority
src/App.test.tsx::does not conflict a dirty page on a legacy watcher echo of our own write
src/App.test.tsx::still conflicts a dirty page on a legacy watcher event that really changed it

entries.notes: Martin, managed graph, deployed 263f8c21: editing a block and then moving it up QUICKLY raised the top-bar banner ““Tine” changed on disk (edited elsewhere or synced in). Your unsaved changes weren’t written.” Doing the same slowly did not. No external writer was involved. Root cause: the managed runtime emits sparse-v2-changed (src-tauri/src/watcher.rs) on every completed tick, and the tick (SyncRuntimeTick, crates/tine-core/src/sync_runtime.rs:1448) carries only epoch: u64 — no page, no origin — and fires for AdmittedNoop, which by name changed nothing. handleSparseV2Changed then asked reloadDisposition, which returns "conflict" for isDirty || isConflicted || isSaving, and called markConflict. So a contentless aggregate signal plus a dirty page produced a conflict with nothing compared. The harm is not cosmetic: doSave refuses a conflicted page, so the banner's own claim became true only because of the banner, and it blocked the very save whose base_rev guard would have decided the question correctly. reloadDisposition conflates two judgments — “do not overwrite the in-memory edit” (always right for a dirty page) and “declare a conflict” (needs proof this page diverged). Fix: divergedFromBaseline(name, stored) in persistence.ts compares the stored page's content revision against the editor's baseline across all four quadrants (equal revision = our own echo, not diverged; different revision = diverged; absent with a baseline = deleted under us, diverged; absent with no baseline = never-written page, not diverged). An in-flight save is skipped entirely: its own base_rev guard is the authority and decides against the exact bytes it is writing. The same proof is applied to the legacy watcher path in handleGraphChange, where Tine's save normally suppresses its own echo but a synced/polled graph or a self-write-marker gap can still surface one (see store.upsertPage). Fail-before proven by reverting only the two production files and rerunning the new tests: the three false-conflict tests failed, and the three “still conflicts” guards passed both before and after, so they are not vacuous. Frontend-integration layer: the real-app reproduction depends on watcher timing and was not reproduced natively; the mechanism was reproduced deterministically at the frontend observation boundary. Follow-up not taken here: give the tick page identity and origin in the backend so the frontend does not have to re-derive per-page divergence from a contentless signal, and consider not emitting sparse-v2-changed for AdmittedNoop at all. 2026-08-07 (021e21a8): the backend half, owed since the frontend repair. The watcher emitted sparse-v2-changed for both admitted tick variants, but AdmittedNoop is by construction the drain step that took no completed batch. So a quiet admission woke the frontend with a contentless signal, which is what a dirty page then read as a conflict against nothing. Only AdmittedComplete now reports a change, via a named and unit-tested predicate in core rather than an inline match in the watcher loop. divergedFromBaseline is unchanged and still required: a tick still names no page and carries no origin, so per-page proof remains the authority.

entries.title: Crash reopen of a lived-in managed graph does not re-resolve one whole-graph manifest per page
entries.notes: Martin reported unsafe reopen of his real managed graph spending about 63.6 s in RecoveringPromotedRuntime. The existing managed_crash_reopen_real_graph_manual_benchmark could not see it: it reopens a graph activated seconds earlier, so its oplog holds one generation (195 ms accelerated, 2.5 s forced-full-replay). The missing variable was aged history. managed_crash_reopen_aged_history_manual_benchmark adds it — N accepted saves across N pages, each fully drained so the local journal crosses its compaction threshold repeatedly, then one pending save and an unsafe drop — and reproduces 72.2 s on the 1,046-file anonymized graph. Localization by successive splitting, each step measured rather than inferred: the reopen rebuilds the disposable projection (projection_recovery=rebuilt-preserving-evidence, reason 'SQLite projection files differ from their authenticated checkpoint'), but the rebuild's own SQLite work is under 0.5 s and forensic preservation is 0.16 ms; 99.6% is materialize_accepted_event_with_stats, and inside that 83% is validate_external_record_anchor at about 30 ms per document. Cause: anchor validation needs the manifest per document, and every document of one bootstrap batch names the same source batch, but load_observed_manifest was called per document — cloning a manifest carrying a descriptor per document, or reloading and revalidating the entire retained bootstrap part off disk, once per page. load_archive_document_object then reloaded that same retained part a second time per document and linearly scanned every object in it. Two whole-graph costs per page, so quadratic in graph size. Fixed by memoizing both for the SAME public operation as the existing status/anchor point caches (cleared together in begin_point_operation, bounded at 4 batches, cleared wholesale at the cap because correctness never depends on a hit), plus a document -> CrdtUpdate index built once per memoized part. This memoizes only WHERE a manifest was found, never WHETHER a record matches it: every document still proves its own descriptor content digest and manifest fingerprint. Measured on the same commit pair: 1,046 files 72,229 ms -> 19,751 ms total and 69,911 ms -> 17,390 ms sqlite_open; 350 files 12,230 -> 3,428; 100 files 2,101 -> 874. Anchor validation 31.6 s -> 0.86 s. tine-core release suite 2030 passed with the same 15 pre-existing failures as master (doc::promoted_heading_tests and model::tests::write_highlights_*, all unrelated and failing identically before the change). STILL OPEN, deliberately not claimed fixed here: the remaining cost is superlinear too — per-document scratch LSM lookups in load_external_exact run without a ScratchLookupSession, unlike the bootstrap bulk materializer which threads one; and the reopen still re-materializes about twice the graph because compacted generations replay whole-graph slices (240/453/220/78 pages for eight single-page edits). Also unaddressed: why the projection is invalidated at all after ordinary drained saves. The regression guard is a 45 s tripwire inside the manual benchmark, which is NOT a CI gate; a counter-based assertion that manifest resolutions are bounded per batch rather than per document would be the durable guard.

entries.title: Unsafe reopen opens a projection already at the accepted frontier instead of rebuilding the whole graph
entries.notes: Unsafe reopen of a lived-in managed graph rebuilt the ENTIRE SQLite projection even though that projection was already exactly at the oplog's accepted frontier. Established by evidence, not inference: the single rebuild reason string in validate_projection_checkpoint collapsed three independent bindings into one message; split apart, the one that fired was 'checkpoint names a different frontier root'. A field-by-field probe of the two AcceptedFrontierRoot values then showed exactly ONE differing field: scratch_root. Every authenticated field -- acceptance_sequence, document_map_root_digest, batch_map_root_digest, reference_catalog_root, state_digest -- was identical. scratch_root is a run-local address for where THIS process keeps the frontier's maps; next_accepted_frontier_root never hashes it into state_digest, and the type's own doc comment calls it a run-local scratch-store reference. Reopening a graph moves it as a matter of course. Because it sat inside the derived PartialEq and inside canonical_frontier_root_bytes (postcard of the whole struct), it also propagated into every durable identity derived from those bytes -- the projection checkpoint, the materialization stamp, the stored frontier row -- so a correct, up-to-date projection compared unequal to the very frontier it was already at, and recovery could only read that as corruption and answer by discarding the database and replaying the whole accepted history. Fixed by CUTTING the pointer out of identity rather than by making the rebuild faster: a hand-written PartialEq for AcceptedFrontierRoot that compares the authenticated fields only, and canonical_frontier_root_bytes stripping scratch_root so no persisted digest can depend on where this process happened to put things. Measured on the same commit pair, full anonymized 1,046-file graph: total reopen 72,229 ms -> 2,138 ms, sqlite_open 69,911 ms -> 3.1 ms, projection_recovery rebuilt-preserving-evidence -> opened-existing with 0 batches applied and 0 pages materialized. 350 files 12,230 -> 1,261; 100 files 2,101 -> 598. sqlite_open is now flat (about 3-6 ms) at every graph size instead of about n^1.6. Also landed, diagnosis-only: the three checkpoint bindings now report separately, and validate_existing validates the database against its OWN sequence and distinguishes 'behind the oplog' from 'diverged from the oplog' (both still rebuild; they are no longer reported with the same words). A catch-up path that would apply only the missing batches was written and then REMOVED before landing: with the identity cut in place it never runs (applied_batches=0), and shipping an unexercised recovery posture on the data-safety path is the opposite of cutting. Guard: managed_unsafe_reopen_at_the_accepted_frontier_opens_without_rebuilding is a NON-ignored CI test asserting on counters (projection_recovery == opened-existing, 0 applied batches, 0 materialized pages) rather than elapsed time, so a return of the defect fails on any machine. Fail-before proven by reverting ONLY the two production hunks: the gate failed with 'a projection already at the accepted frontier was not opened as-is (reason: SQLite frontier is stale)'. tine-core release suite 2031 passed with exactly the same 15 pre-existing failures as master (failure sets diffed, byte-identical). Note on suite noise: the oplog::local_active ephemeral-retention test family is load-flaky on master too (reproduced on unmodified master under CPU load); the new gate adds contention and raises how often it is seen. STILL OPEN: the remaining 2.1 s is engine_open, not the projection; per-document scratch LSM lookups in load_external_exact still run without a ScratchLookupSession.

entries.title: External edits to pages outside journals/ and pages/ reach the open app instead of staying invisible until reopen
entries.notes: Discovery went graph-wide in the #246 fix; watcher event routing did not follow. The OS watch was already installed recursively on the graph ROOT, so events for a page at the root or in a custom folder arrived correctly -- and were then discarded by the reconcile lane, which filtered pending paths against [journals/, pages/] and built its diff snapshot from those two directories only. Such a page was therefore listed at open and never updated again while the app stayed open. Fixed by giving the watcher the same authority discovery uses (GraphTextScope), via Graph::graph_text_watch_relevant / _descend / _could_contain. Fail-before proven by restoring the two pre-fix predicates in place: the snapshot returned only [journals/2026_08_06.md, pages/Page.md] against an expected five, and event routing returned only [pages/Page.md] against an expected three. Conflict copies stay routed (they are not eligible text but must refresh the conflicts panel); excluded trees (assets/, dot-directories, logseq/bak/) stay excluded on both the routing and the force-a-full-scan paths, so dropping an image into assets/ still cannot trigger a graph rescan. Freshness defect only, not write-safety: the pre-debounce write-guard lane always saw every event and stayed fail-closed.

entries.title: A network-share (poll-mode) graph keeps its save-time admission index warm instead of rebuilding the whole graph on every save
entries.notes: When the watcher runs in poll mode (a network share, or TINE_WATCH=poll), every 3 s cycle invalidated the guarded graph-text admission index unconditionally before reconciling. Since a Direct save consults that index and rebuilds it when invalid -- a two-pass byte-retaining walk of the whole graph -- such a user could never hold a warm index and paid a full-graph rebuild on essentially every save. The blanket invalidation was compensating for the poll rescan being narrower than the index (journals/+pages/ vs graph-wide); once REG-EXTERNAL-GRAPH-WIDE-EVENTS-268 widened the rescan to the same scope, the rescan's own result became a complete account of what changed and is published as exact observations instead. Ordering is load-bearing and asserted: the observation happens after the scan and BEFORE any reconcile, so the index is never staler than the scan that produced it -- the same window the inotify callback lane already had, not a wider one. A scan that could not read part of the graph reports itself incomplete and still invalidates. Fail-before proven by restoring the blanket invalidation in place: the quiet-cycle test then reported invalidated: true with complete_builds unchanged at 1.

entries.title: Saving an existing page never captures or reparses the whole graph
entries.notes: Reopened after the reporter confirmed the defect remained in v0.6.91 Direct Files. The diagnostic refusal was `precheck.limit: guarded graph-text identity construction failed: initial shadow peak build memory bound exceeded`; GH #295 independently measured one complete 1,046-file / 16.7 MB capture on every Windows save (roughly 0.9-1.1 s). Root cause was architectural: both existing-target validation and the atomic replacement transaction invoked the complete managed shadow-import admission index. The cut now keeps an existing save local: one exact target parse/read, one capability-safe traversal following only portable-equivalent target path components (including case/NFC aliases in ancestor directories), exact file identity and link-count-one checks, and the existing no-replace/retire/restore/fsync protocol. Missing-target creation alone retains the complete semantic proof and its parsed-semantic reuse. On the attached #295 graph in release mode, warm save median was 1.13 ms and forcibly invalidated save median 0.98 ms, with complete builds unchanged at one; the prior current-master measurement was 2.75 ms warm and 70 ms invalidated. Structural tests prove exactly one portable traversal, zero graph capture enumerations, one target parse, and no write on portable/hard-link/external-byte conflicts.

entries.title: A page whose file was replaced with identical content can still be saved instead of stranding the edit
entries.notes: A save proves it is not clobbering someone else's work two ways: base_rev must still match the bytes on disk, AND the file must still be the same physical file read at load. External tools break the second without touching the first -- OneDrive rehydrating a Files-On-Demand placeholder, a Syncthing pull landing identical bytes, cp over a hardlink. Every later save then failed with 'existing page identity changed since load', and BOTH exits from the resulting conflict prompt were dead ends: Keep-mine re-ran the same check and failed too, and Use-disk-version discarded the user's edit. The watcher now re-pins the retained identity when, and only when, the retained revision still matches the bytes now on disk, so the proof it stands on is unchanged. Fail-before proven by disabling the re-pin in place. The control (a replace that also changes the bytes) still conflicts and still writes nothing, and is asserted alongside.

entries.title: A symlink inside the graph does not make every other page unsaveable
entries.notes: One symlink in a descended, non-excluded scope (graph root, pages/, journals/, a custom folder) aborted the save-time admission capture, and because every Direct save takes that capture to answer a filename question, the whole graph became read-only -- the user's OTHER pages could not be saved either. Skipping is what the rest of Tine already does: every traversal is no-follow, the watcher snapshot never descends a symlinked directory, and graph_inventory_entry never admits a symlinked file, so the capture was the only place escalating a non-entity to a fatal error. The shadow-import bootstrap capture still refuses, asserted separately: an import that silently leaves out a file the user considers part of their graph is a worse failure than a refused import. NOTE the audit's own repro for this finding is WRONG -- it used assets/, which is fixed-excluded, so that experiment goes green and would retire a real finding; both halves are asserted in one test so nobody re-runs it. Known bounded gap: a symlink is no longer a member of the portable-key collision group, matching discovery, which never knew about it either.

entries.title: Save failures that a conflict prompt cannot resolve are reported as themselves, not as a content conflict
entries.notes: The backend collapsed EVERY io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists to the literal string 'conflict', and the frontend recognised a conflict by testing whether the message CONTAINED that substring. A portable-filename collision, a physical-resource alias, a symlink refusal and 'another document owns this page identity' therefore all raised the content-conflict prompt, whose only options are Keep-mine and Use-disk-version -- neither of which can resolve any of them. Choosing either left the page marked conflicted, and a conflicted page silently refuses to save from then on, so the user's page was stranded by an error message. Only a real base-revision conflict carries the 'conflict' contract now; everything else carries its bounded D0 failure code as a stable prefix and falls through to the retryable path. The frontend match is exact rather than substring. Fail-before is structural and asserted directly on the mapping function.

entries.title: A sync client touching an unrelated file does not fail the save in progress
entries.notes: The save-time admission capture runs two full-graph passes that must agree exactly, and ANY concurrent filesystem activity anywhere in the graph makes them disagree. On a Syncthing / Dropbox / OneDrive folder that is not an anomaly, it is the steady state -- and a single disagreement surfaced as a failed save. Disagreement means 'something moved while we looked', not 'the graph is broken', so it is now retried in place up to 4 attempts; every other error still surfaces immediately, and the caller holds the identity-mutation authority across all attempts so this cannot interleave with one of our own writes. Fail-before proven by setting CAPTURE_ATTEMPTS to 1.

entries.title: A save failure a retry cannot change is reported once instead of re-running the whole check three times

tests: src/persistence.test.ts::does not retry failures a retry cannot change

entries.notes: scheduleTransientRetry re-ran a failed save at 100 ms and 300 ms before toasting -- three full attempts per dirty page. Each attempt re-runs the whole pre-save admission check, which on a large graph is the expensive part, only to reach the same answer for a failure class that cannot change on retry: a portable-filename collision, a physical-resource alias, a symlink in scope, a non-portable path, a nofollow refusal, a limit breach, or another page already owning the title. #267's 'about a minute, then a red toast' is that multiplier on top of an already slow check. Those classes now report once; genuinely transient ones (precheck.interrupted, identity.changed_since_load, unclassified I/O) still retry. Depends on REG-SAVE-ERROR-MISCLASSIFIED-AS-CONFLICT-001 for the bounded codes that make the distinction possible.

entries.title: Resolving a save conflict with "keep mine" overwrites the file, including after a real external change
entries.notes: force_save_page proved its right to write the pinned file from PageDto.rev, which pageToDto never sets -- ordinary saves carry the load revision in the separate base_rev argument, as the parameter's own comment said. With rev=None the retained-owner check could not hold, so every override failed AlreadyExists 'path-pinned page does not match its captured exact owner', leaving discard-my-edits as the only working exit from the conflict prompt. The suite missed it because every test force-saved a load_named/load_by_path DTO, which does carry rev=Some -- a shape the wire never produces. Replaced the untyped revision argument with an explicit PinnedSaveAuthority. Audit 2026-08-06 N1 (Critical).

entries.title: An unclassified save failure reports what happened instead of raising an unresolvable conflict prompt
entries.notes: direct_save_failure_code ended with a catch-all mapping any AlreadyExists to conflict.other, which commands.rs turned into the literal 'conflict' -- the string that raises the keep-mine/use-disk banner. About forty-five other conditions raise AlreadyExists (managed and projection internals, reservation and page-name collisions) for which neither button helps and 'use disk' discards the user's edits; the mapping also replaced the message text, so a failure that had RETAINED those edits under a recovery name arrived as a bare unexplained conflict. conflict.* membership is now decided by naming a condition. Audit 2026-08-06 N3 (High) and the still-open half of N2.

entries.title: A conflict resolution during a cross-page move waits for the destination write instead of writing the moved block out of existence

tests: src/persistenceMoveBarrier.test.ts::defers a keep-mine on a held source, then applies it on release

entries.notes: heldSources holds a moved subtree's SOURCE pages until the DESTINATION write is durable, so the block is never in neither place. The guard read heldSources.has(name) && !force, so a forced save walked through it. Latent while force-save could not reach the backend (N1); live once it could. A deferred keep-mine is now remembered and re-issued when the destination lands, because the ordinary save path skips a conflicted page and dropping it would strand the resolution. Audit 2026-08-06 N6.

entries.title: External changes to a Tine-managed graph reconcile instead of being refused to the retry limit
entries.notes: The drain proves a durable receipt still describes the accepted state by replaying it and comparing intents; the receipt is written WITH authenticated annotations and the replay runs WITHOUT them. plan_exact_source_projection compared whole annotations, whose spans come from two producers with different conventions over the same bytes: marker instrumentation ends a block before its line terminator, block tiling runs to the start of the next block and includes it. One save through the fall-through branch wrote tiling spans into the receipt, which then became the next save's authenticated base and could never match a fresh render, so every later save took the fall-through while the replay always took the rendered route. Now compares identities and lets spans be re-derived. Bisected to 547f8713, which is correct and was NOT reverted. Eight sync_runtime tests were one defect.

entries.title: A refused managed save reports the refusal instead of retrying silently forever

tests: src/persistence.test.ts::does not retry failures a retry cannot change

entries.notes: A managed conflict returned 'conflict: {Reason}'. The frontend compares the conflict string exactly, so it matched neither the banner nor any bounded code and fell into the transient-retry path -- retried on a timer, never surfaced, and the user could quit believing the page was written. Now carries a managed.conflict code the frontend treats as permanent, with a message saying to reload. Deliberately not the bare 'conflict': force is hard-refused while managed storage is active, so that banner's only working button would be the one that discards the user's edits. A real managed resolution path is a product decision and remains open as audit M2's second half. Audit 2026-08-06 M2 (High) and M5.

entries.title: A managed rename on Windows refuses to replace a file that appears between the check and the rename
entries.notes: rename_managed_noreplace used renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) on Linux/Android and renameatx_np(RENAME_EXCL) on macOS/BSD, but Dir::rename on Windows -- which cap-std implements with replace semantics, so the one guarantee its name makes was the one Windows did not provide. Now delegates to rename_projection_between_noreplace, which renames an opened DELETE-access handle with FileRenameInformation and ReplaceIfExists=FALSE and rejects filesystems lacking the primitive before retiring the live source name. Compile-verified for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu locally; behaviour is proved by the Windows CI job, so confidence is partial by design. Audit 2026-08-06 M3.

entries.title: A cleanly shut down managed graph never opens again if its disposable SQLite projection is lost or damaged
entries.notes: A Safe (clean-shutdown) reopen used reopen_promoted_local_runtime_existing_projection, which refused a missing or invalid projection instead of rebuilding it, while the crash path already rebuilt the same state. So the tidier lifecycle was the unrecoverable one: deleting the cache (cleared cache directory, sweeper, restore that skipped it) or leaving it unreadable (corruption, schema-version bump) left the graph permanently unopenable, reported to the frontend as Retryable -- a retry button that can never succeed. The projection is a frontier-stamped disposable cache of an authoritative oplog per ADR 0049, so losing it is recoverable by definition. The Safe path now uses reopen_promoted_local_runtime (AllowRebuild) and the existing-only entry point is deleted; ExistingOnly survives only for the same-process handoff, where the projection is held open by this very process. A present, current projection still opens as-is. Fail-before: both tests fail on the parent commit with OpenRefused.

entries.title: Rebuilding a managed graph's projection cost about n^1.6, so a large graph spent minutes on a recovery a small one did in a second
entries.notes: AcceptedRootMaterializer -- the materializer a projection rebuild actually uses -- held no scratch lookup sessions, while BootstrapBulkMaterializer held two. Every document resolution therefore re-walked the scratch LSM from the top, and the LSM grows with the graph, so per-document cost rose with graph size even though the number of document loads stayed linear (2.17, 2.04, 1.96 loads per file at 100/350/1045 files). Measured on the anonymized corpus: 388 ms / 2,214 ms / 14,976 ms, i.e. exponent 1.46 then 1.76, against Martin's stated ceiling of 10 s and truly linear. After giving the materializer the same two root-bound sessions: 271 ms / 796 ms / 2,627 ms, exponent 0.86 then 1.09. Sessions change only how bytes are reached; every record still proves its own anchor, peer counters and direct heads. The guard asserts session hits exceed misses rather than a wall-clock budget, because a small CI fixture is fast whatever the routing -- which is how this went unnoticed. Fail-before: 0 hits, 0 misses over 128 document loads.

entries.title: An unread catalog-root stamp in the page-alias table made two correct builds of the same graph disagree
entries.notes: reference_alias_bindings carried a catalog_root_digest column that every write path set and no read path ever consulted -- both production reads select resolved_page_id filtered by normalized_alias only. Because it sat in the primary key and the row digest, it made an incrementally drained database and a rebuilt one disagree on a page they resolved identically: the drain stamps the catalog root current when the alias was last touched, a rebuild stamps the root it resolved at. Dumped rows confirmed same alias, same ordinal, same resolved page, different stamp, while both databases carried the same materialization_stamp. Column dropped from the table, its primary key, its index and the digested column list; SQLITE_SCHEMA_VERSION 11 -> 12, so each managed graph rebuilds its projection once. The projection's own materialization_stamp already records the catalog root the whole database is at, which is the question anyone actually asks. Fail-before: format_identity_is_pinned caught the version change immediately, which is what it is for.

entries.title: Linked/Unlinked References, search, quick switch, {{query}}, aliases, templates and asset reads work while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Martin reported "Couldn't load references because the backend request failed." on every page of a managed graph. Root cause was authority, not references: GraphSlot exposed only legacy write authority, so with_graph refused all ~50 read-only commands under managed storage and only six page-path commands worked. Reads now go through with_read_graph, served for managed bindings by a Graph opened with open_derived_read_only over the projected tree. That view fails every graph-text write at admit_managed_text_writer and ensure_write_target, so a misrouted write command errors instead of writing behind the oplog; assets stay writable because assets/ is outside the oplog's document domain. Writes (rename, delete, merge, config setters, conflict resolution) remain refused under managed storage and still need real oplog implementations.

entries.title: Every Settings toggle persists while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Favorites, preferred workflow, preferred format, journal title format, start of week, show brackets, logical outdenting, doc-mode Enter, time tracking, default journal template and the guide-announced flag all silently failed under Tine-managed storage: the eleven set_* commands went through with_graph, the authority that answers "may this caller write graph text", and a managed binding correctly says no. Settled from source that graph configuration is NOT oplog-owned: the reconciliation scanner classifies logseq/config.edn as GraphTextScanPathClass::Configuration (model.rs, capture_reconciliation_scan_pass) and reconciliation_baseline_adapter.rs::scan_file_row drops those rows as "not managed content" that "cannot be represented as a ManagedPath", so nothing imports, projects or reconciles it; config bytes only join the within-scan two-pass stability digest. sync_runtime.rs:17310, the line that raised the question, is a test fixture's filesystem walk and says nothing about the oplog's domain. Fix: a Graph::ensure_config_write_target capability narrowed to that one exact path, and a with_config_graph route at the command layer. refresh_graph now takes a managed branch that rebuilds the read-only view instead of reopening a legacy graph, because a Graph reads config.edn when it opens. The same branch refreshes the GraphMeta snapshot the slot hands back, which load_graph returns verbatim when a window reloads the root it already holds; without it a saved setting looked reverted on the next load. The legacy path gets that for free by publishing a replacement slot. Still not done under managed storage: set_journal_title_format does not migrate journal filenames, since that is a rename the oplog owns.

entries.title: Orphaned assets can be trashed and the asset trash emptied while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: trash_asset and empty_asset_trash were refused under managed storage only incidentally: the asset itself passed ensure_asset_write_target, but the destination directory went through ensure_write_target, which the read-only view refuses along with graph text. Settled from source that the trash tree is outside the oplog's document domain: graph_text_scope.rs::fixed_excluded lists logseq/.tine-trash beside assets, publish and .tine-sync, so nothing under it is scanned, imported or projected. Fix: Graph::ensure_trash_write_target, used by the four asset-side trash destinations, plus a with_trash_graph route. Page, journal and conflict trashing is unaffected and still refused, because its SOURCE is graph text and it goes through admit_managed_text_writer.

entries.title: Page rename/delete/merge, conflict resolution, guide copy and native capture work while Tine-managed storage is active
entries.notes: Remaining half of the 2026-08-07 authority defect. The read half is REG-MANAGED-WHOLE-GRAPH-READS-REFUSED-001 (25f36f16); settings and the asset trash are REG-MANAGED-SETTINGS-WRITES-REFUSED-001 and REG-MANAGED-ASSET-TRASH-REFUSED-001. Still refused under managed storage, needing real oplog transactions: rename_page, delete_page, merge_pages, rename_file_to_page, resolve_sync_conflict, trash_sync_conflict, trash_journal_file, copy_guide_into_graph. The enumeration this row asked for now exists: src-tauri/src/managed_command_surface.rs lists all 141 Tauri commands with the routing each one uses, re-derives that routing from the sources, and fails when the refused set changes -- so a new command that cannot work under managed storage is a failing diff rather than a user report. That enumeration surfaced a group nobody had listed: publish_html, open_pdf, read_highlights, write_highlights, write_pdf_view_state, save_pdf_area_image, save_asset and stream_asset_path are all asset/publish-domain work, outside the oplog's document domain, still sitting on the legacy write authority. They are the cheapest remaining slice. Tracked as M5 in specs/handoffs/2026-08-06-direct-files-program.md.

entries.title: Images and streamed media can be read from nested assets directories
entries.notes: The frontend already reduced ./assets/dir/file.png to the assets-relative name dir/file.png, but all native read entry points applied the top-level-only validator used by asset creation. Read paths now accept ordinary nested relative components and retain canonical containment beneath the approved assets root. Absolute paths, empty/dot/parent components, portable backslash traversal and symlink escapes remain refused. Asset creation/import still accepts only a top-level filename.

entries.title: Opening a large Direct Files graph does not synchronously scan its pages or assets
entries.notes: The reporter measured 44.9 seconds inside the frontend load_graph call on Windows for about 13,000 pages and 25,884 files / 24.6 GB. The representative release benchmark creates 13,000 Markdown pages plus 12,884 sparse assets in 281 buckets (25.2 GiB apparent assets): current core open took 0.4 ms and the full current Linux app returned from load_graph in 65 ms; the released v0.6.90 Linux AppImage returned in 26 ms on the same fixture. Graph size alone therefore does not reproduce the Windows report. Debug builds now emit phase and cumulative timings for canonicalization, private/shared storage discovery, asset approval, Direct core open, legacy store discovery, graph binding, backup scheduling, settings/title, and warm-cache scheduling. The focused Windows WebView2 scenario measures the load_graph interval on the same file-count shape and preserves phase diagnostics, but cannot duplicate the reporter's physical disk, antivirus, or 24.6 GB of real payload. Keep this reported until a current Windows trace identifies the missing filesystem or platform phase.

entries.title: Managed storage activation on a large Windows graph either becomes active or leaves Direct Files usable
entries.notes: The reporter saw activation fail on Windows 11 with about 13,000 pages, after which pages were unavailable until returning to Direct Files. The focused hosted-Windows WebView2 scenario drives the real Settings activation on a 13,000-page nested Unicode Markdown/Org graph, verifies byte-preserved source files, opens a nested page under managed storage, returns to Direct Files, and reopens the page. Keep this reported until hosted execution either reproduces the failure or records a repeatable pass that sharply narrows the remaining Windows 11 or graph-content evidence gap.

entries.title: A fresh checkout has no tracked paths that collide on a case-insensitive filesystem
entries.notes: docs/UI-REGRESSION-TESTING.md is the current referenced execution contract; the case-only lowercase twin was an older planning document with no references and caused Git to omit one file on Windows checkout. The obsolete twin is removed, and the release-pipeline contract now folds every tracked path through NFC plus lowercase and refuses future collisions.

entries.title: Editing one block does not rewrite bytes belonging to blocks the user never touched
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 3, reproduced and re-measured independently: editing one block and reverting it failed to restore the bytes of 96 of 983 files (9.8%) on a copy of ~/research/logseq-anonymized. 88 of the 96 were an unbulleted page-level '## Heading' gaining a '- ' prefix; the worst shape injected the source layout whitespace ('\t  ') into the block TEXT and added a nesting level. Root cause was not the parser: doc.rs's source-layout retention machinery existed but every production call site passed an empty StructuralLayoutIdentity slice, so identity_bound_unbulleted_headings was always empty and the retention was inert on the Direct save path (test-only). doc::layout_identities_of now reads the locator->identity map off the document tree and serialize_page_dto_for_path passes it. Corpus after the fix: 96 damaged -> 0; unchanged-save no-op still byte-exact at 1045/0. Residual, backlogged: a whitespace-only separator line normalises to empty, which is why the continuation-heading test asserts text and depth rather than exact bytes.

entries.title: A content-only save keeps the physical page inventory warm instead of forcing a whole-graph re-read
entries.notes: Direct Files perf audit 2026-08-09, F1, found independently by both the Opus and Codex lanes with agreeing numbers (243 ms vs 263-281 ms). list_pages is memoized on raw cache_gen and its only rebuild path walks the graph text scope, re-reads every file and re-parses each one: ~35 us/file, linear from 506 to 8,006 pages, and find_entry rebuilds straight from it. Every save bumped the generation, so the first navigation or [[ autocomplete after any typing pause stalled ~1/4 s on a real 5,225-file graph. page_list_cache is now re-tagged to the new generation under the same condition the effective-identity index already uses. DELIBERATELY NARROWER than the auditor's recommendation: list_pages parses every file so a title:: edit really does move an entry (hence the !identity_changed gate), and referenced_page_names is genuinely content-derived and is left to rebuild. The test asserts a ratio, not an absolute time, so it survives a loaded shared box.

entries.title: Pending edits are written when the app is backgrounded or hidden, not only on a clean window close
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 7. The ONLY durability barrier in the app was onCloseRequested. Android/iOS never send one - the OS backgrounds the app and reclaims it later - so everything inside the 400ms save debounce was RAM-only. The three pre-existing visibilitychange listeners (Page.tsx, journal.ts, assetRefresh.ts) all act on becoming VISIBLE; this is the other edge. FAIL-BEFORE is an absence, not a wrong value: no listener flushed on hide, verified by grep across the tree, so there is no pre-fix test that can fail. Confidence for #255 is therefore MODERATE, not high: this is the plainest explanation for the Android half and is a real missing handler, but no same-platform reproduction of the reporter's loss exists. Findings 2 and 6 are other live candidates for the same report.

entries.title: A dirty page name with no page behind it no longer wedges every later flush
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 6. doSave bailed on a null DTO BEFORE dirty.delete(name), so the name stayed dirty forever and flushAll() could never return true again: every graph switch aborted with 'Some pages couldn't be saved' and every window close offered to discard edits that were already on disk. Reachable because pinnedPages() did not pin in-flight saves - doSave removes a page from dirty before awaiting, so the working-set cap could evict it mid-write, and a transient failure then re-added a name with no page. Two parts: savingPages() is now pinned (prevents the eviction outright), and a dirty name with no page in the store is dropped rather than wedging. Deliberately NOT dropped when the page exists but the page-header firewall refused the DTO - that is a real unsaved edit and must keep blocking.

entries.title: A watcher-driven disk reload re-checks safety at the moment it applies, not before its IPC
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 5. reloadDisposition is correct, but all four watcher sites read its verdict and then awaited backend().getPage(...) before acting - tens to hundreds of ms on a large graph, and a Syncthing burst fires many concurrently. Text typed inside that window was destroyed: upsertPage replaced the page, dropping the edit AND its undo history, with no conflict raised and nothing written to disk. store.upsertUnlessDirty already re-checked at the moment of the upsert; only these sites skipped it. reloadPageIfStillSafe re-checks centrally so a fifth watcher site cannot reintroduce the hole. reloadPage itself is deliberately left as a clobber - 'use disk version' is an explicit user decision.

entries.title: Deleting a page does its graph-wide work on the blocking pool, not the command thread
entries.notes: Direct Files perf audit 2026-08-09, F3. delete_page re-derives the page inventory and rebuilds three O(pages) indexes: measured ~95 us/file, linear, 757 ms at 8,006 files and ~1.9 s projected at 20,000. It was the only such command still running synchronously on the command thread; get_page, save_page and rename_page already cross the blocking pool. The guard test expensive_reference_and_rename_commands_cross_the_blocking_pool existed and simply did not list delete_page - a coverage omission, not a missing mechanism. This does not make delete faster; it stops it freezing command dispatch. The O(graph) cost itself is a separate, still-open finding.

entries.title: An ordinary save after an external atomic replacement compares bytes instead of refusing on physical identity
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 1, ordinary save only. An external editor that writes by temp+rename (the common safe pattern, and what Syncthing/Dropbox deliver) leaves the same path on a NEW inode. save_page authorized with PinnedSaveAuthority::LoadedRevision, whose retained-identity check refused before the byte comparison ever ran, returning 'path-pinned page does not match its captured exact owner' - a message isRetryableSaveFailure retries forever, so the page became permanently unsaveable with no user-resolvable path out. Measured pre-fix: 4 of 5 cases fail, and NOTABLY the different-byte case failed with the same unresolvable code, so a genuine external change was equally unrecoverable, not just the same-byte one. A new authority OrdinaryEditorSave proves exact path ownership and nothing about physical identity; the byte comparison then decides. Equal bytes on a new inode re-pin to the current snapshot and proceed; different bytes return the literal 'conflict' the frontend can resolve. LoadedRevision is UNCHANGED and still used by verify_existing_journal_page_projection, which authenticates before an opaque durable append and must not inherit this reorder - the contract verifier rejected a helper-wide change twice on exactly this boundary. At increment 1, delete conflicts and the force-save half were deliberately deferred to increment 2; the next record covers both.

entries.title: Keep mine writes only over the exact disk snapshot shown by its conflict
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 2. A conflict now mints one per-Graph, per-editor-episode, exact-path, monotonic-epoch token holding Present { revision, resource_identity } or Absent plus the coherently observed baseline bytes. Force consumes it before every attempt and runs the ordinary save protocol with those bytes and identity substituted as its rechecked baseline; it never delegates by revision alone. Under Martin's state-not-events ruling (2026-08-09) a byte-identical republication of the shown snapshot is a no-op, so force DOES rebind to the live inode in exactly that case and refuses a different-byte winner on a new inode; two tests pin both halves. S1-S9 each have a deterministic site test, including both final-reread arms and post-restore/post-publication observation timing. Stable observations get per-site conflict.* codes; exceptional observation failure gets conflict_retry.*, which cannot reach the keep-mine/use-disk banner and now also RETRACTS an existing one: a force has already spent its token by then, so leaving the banner up left Keep-mine permanently dead beside a destructive Use-disk (adversarial implementation verification, finding 3). Loads, watcher observations, forget_file, successful saves, and the shared Tine-owned graph-text mutation boundary revoke authority, covering rename/delete/trash/merge, managed projection/import/migration, sync-conflict resolution, and PDF-highlight page writes. Hard admission refusals remain tokenless.

entries.title: Unlinked References finds a page name written inside code, math and other literal text
entries.notes: Logseq matches unlinked references with a raw regex over the whole block content (db/model.cljs get-page-unlinked-references, only drawer/remove-logbook stripped), so code fences, inline code, math, raw HTML, examples, latex environments and hiccup are all searched. Tine derived its search region from an ALLOWLIST of block kinds in reference_evidence walk_blocks, whose `_ => {}` arm silently dropped every other variant - so the region lost coverage each time lsdoc grew a block type. Now derived by SUBTRACTION: plain_search_ranges takes the complement of what the parser already claimed (explicit refs, block refs, structural properties, :LOGBOOK: drawers), which is Logseq's own semantics reached through the parser rather than a second scanner - alias/NFC/boundary logic unchanged and new lsdoc variants covered for free. Logseq's `#`/doubled-`[` prefix rule had to be ported explicitly (og_prefix_allows): it used to be implied by overlap with a parsed reference, but inside a fence there is no parsed reference, so `[[Page]]` in code would otherwise have matched. That also corrected an inversion - for `\[[Target]]` Tine reported the escaped bracket and hid both code mentions, exactly backwards from Logseq. DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, named: structural id::/collapsed::/logseq.* property text stays withheld (Logseq scans it) because a page named after a uuid fragment is not a real outcome. PERF: widening the region cost +13% (285->325 ms cold on the 1,045-file anonymized graph), so an ASCII prefilter was added to visit_plain_matches - it skips a start position only when BOTH the name's first char and the source char are ASCII, where lowercase is exact and NFC is identity, leaving folding cases like the Kelvin sign to the authoritative matcher. Net 285 ms -> 36 ms, ~8x faster than before the change. Reusing string buffers instead was measured WORSE (400 ms) because flat_map(char::to_lowercase) loses str::to_lowercase's ASCII fast path. Necessity: 6 unit tests and 2 of 3 integration tests fail on the pre-fix tree; the third asserts the complement did NOT over-widen (an explicit link and a CLOCK: line stay out) and passes both sides.

entries.title: A link naming no existing page is visibly distinguished, and a fileless #tag is not
entries.notes: Martin, 2026-08-09: a generated graph wrote each report to `pages/c01 Swap Bribery.md` with `title:: Swap Bribery` and linked the index by FILENAME. Since Logseq resolves a page's name as title:: > filename > first block (graph-parser extract.cljc get-page-name), the filename named nothing and all 29 links opened blank pages with no signal. Tine <=0.6.5 used the filename and ignored title::; aa4a4b29 (2026-07-29, shipped in 0.6.90) corrected that, which is why the graph looked fine when built. Backend was never at fault - load_named returned full content for all 30 pages. DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, approved by Martin: Logseq does NOT distinguish unresolved links (components/block.cljs:548 dims only untitled-page?, i.e. a page that EXISTS under a uuid name); Tine dims them, as Obsidian does. Applied to [[refs]] only, NOT #tags - a tag with no page file is ordinary Logseq usage and dimming those would mark most tags in a normal graph. existing_page_names resolves like load_named (normalized keys + alias table, no PageKind filter, so a link to an existing journal is alive) and costs one memoized page-list read per call; pageExistsBatch coalesces every reference in a tick into one IPC, asks each name once per graph, and treats UNKNOWN AS ALIVE so a page of good links never flashes as dead. Verified on the real 30-page graph: 8/8 refs dimmed before the repair, 0/8 after, all six sampled links clicking through to 24-27 block pages.

entries.title: A fluent typing burst is never written to disk until the typist pauses
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 9. scheduleSave cleared and re-armed a 400 ms timer on every markDirty, with no ceiling, so the debounce fired only during a pause in typing. Measured fail-before: 40 keystrokes at 300 ms intervals - 12 seconds of prose at a pace slower than most people type - produced ZERO writes. A crash, power loss or OOM kill during a long passage therefore lost the whole passage, and the loss window grew with how well the writing was going. Fixed by measuring a MAX_SAVE_DELAY_MS ceiling of 3 s from the FIRST dirty mark of a burst rather than the last, so the bound is on file staleness rather than typing speed; the burst clock restarts whenever no save is armed, which every drain path (flushAll, resetSaveState, the timer itself) already guarantees by nulling saveTimer. Coalescing is unchanged: a short burst still costs exactly one write.

entries.title: "Use disk version" on a page pinned to a specific file loads a different file
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 10. Two files can carry one page NAME - the duplicate-day stray of GH #21, or same-titled pages in different folders - and the editor pins such a page to its exact path so saves write back to the file it was loaded from. ConflictBar's "Use disk version" resolved by NAME (backend getPage), which reaches the backend's canonical owner of that name, so the button silently re-pointed the tab at a different file: the user discarded their edits to THIS file and got someone else's file loaded in its place. Fixed by resolving through getPageByPath whenever the loaded page carries a path - the same idiom store.ts, RightSidebar and LiveRefGroup already use. An absent pinned file drops the page rather than falling back to the name, since that fallback is the same defect; an unpinned (never-saved) page still resolves by name because it has nothing else.

entries.title: Deleting a page with unsaved edits promises a recoverable trash copy that does not contain them
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 18. The delete confirmation said only 'The file moves to the graph's .tine-trash folder', which reads as fully recoverable. The trash receives the FILE, so a dirty page's latest keystrokes - and, provably, EVERY edit on a conflicted page, whose saves are refused by design until the conflict is resolved - are destroyed with nothing to recover from. The prompt now names that outcome when the page is dirty or conflicted, while the user can still answer no; wording is unchanged for a page with nothing unsaved. Deliberately NOT fixed by flushing first: making delete trigger a save is a behavior change with its own risk, and it cannot help the conflicted case at all.

entries.title: Closing offers to discard work that is still being written
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 11. The shared close transaction (desktop window-close and Android root Back) bounded flushAll at a flat 4 s and treated expiry as failure, so a flush that had merely not FINISHED was reported in the same words as one that could never succeed - 'unsaved changes that couldn't be saved... close anyway and lose them?' - inviting the user to throw away a write in progress. A slow or network filesystem, a fsync behind a busy disk, or many dirty pages can exceed 4 s with nothing wrong; on the 1,045-file anonymized corpus a save averages ~7 ms, so the bound is already several hundred pages' worth. The close now races the SAME flush promise twice: at the soft bound it says 'still saving' and grants a 26 s grace period, and only a flush that genuinely finished false, threw, or outlasted the grace period reaches a discard prompt - which now distinguishes 'failed' from 'still-saving' in its wording. The pre-existing test asserted that the timeout case behaved identically to failure, i.e. it encoded the defect; it was split rather than grandfathered.

entries.title: A conflict raised by a transient file removal is never cleared when the file returns
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 17. Raising a conflict was gated on a per-page divergence proof; clearing one was gated on nothing, because only a user's click (or forgetPage) ever cleared a conflict. handleGraphChange's REMOVED branch calls markConflict with no proof at all, so an external editor writing by temp+rename, or a mid-delivery Syncthing pass, could park a page behind the banner permanently. doSave then refuses that page forever, and both banner buttons destroy something: 'Use disk version' the unsaved edit, 'Keep mine' a file it never needed to overwrite. Fixed by making the proof two-directional in ONE owner, applyDivergenceVerdict, used by both observation sites (legacy watcher and sparse-v2 epoch): a negative proof on a currently-conflicted page clears the conflict and reschedules the edit it was freezing. A third site cannot reintroduce the asymmetry. A file that returns with DIFFERENT content still conflicts.

entries.title: The direct shadow-journal rule asked two extensions while its managed twin asked three
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 15, landed as a CONSISTENCY fix with an explicit NEGATIVE result. Graph::is_shadow_journal (direct mode) hard-coded canonical candidates '{stem}.md' and '{stem}.org'; its managed twin managed_is_shadow_journal already asked configured_text_variant_paths, i.e. all of LOGSEQ_TEXT_EXTENSIONS = md/markdown/org. The audit predicted that in a '.markdown' graph a title-named leftover would therefore escape the #21 shadow rule and poison the (kind,name) cache. IT DOES NOT: probes at the observation boundary show load_named and journals_desc both still serve the canonical file for both extensions, because later layers mask the misclassification. The necessity gate is therefore NOT satisfied and no user-visible defect is claimed - the divergence between the two classifiers is real and was removed, and the three new tests pin the #21 rule per extension so that a change in whichever layer is currently masking it cannot silently take the guarantee with it.

entries.title: The All Pages sidebar list scanned the whole page list once per visible row
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F9. pageListLabel disambiguates a row whose display name collides with another page (same title in different folders, or the same stem as .md and .org) by scanning the whole list twice - once for the name, once for the parent sub-path. The sidebar called it per rendered row, so rendering All Pages cost O(rows x pages): measured 21 ms at 5,000 pages and 39 ms at 20,000, for 300 visible rows. pageListLabels now counts both keys in ONE pass and returns a lookup, memoized in Sidebar alongside the existing filter+sort memo. The label RULE is unchanged and the three original correctness tests still pass verbatim. Necessity: the shape tests COUNT element reads through a Proxy rather than timing anything - a linear implementation reads the array once while building the index and never again, a per-row scan reads it once more per row - and both fail against the pre-fix implementation. A first attempt asserted wall-clock and was replaced after it flaked on a loaded box: 47 ms against a 26 ms ceiling with the fix in place. The index is keyed by value, not object identity, so a caller holding a copy of an entry gets the same label.

entries.title: Tine crashes at launch with a backtrace when the app-data home is not writable
entries.notes: Found while working the 2026-08-09 Direct Files audit backlog; reproduced on the stock deployed release binary, so not a regression from that work. Tauri creates the WebView user-data directory ($XDG_DATA_HOME/page.tine.Tine) inside its OWN setup(), while building the configured windows (tauri::manager::webview calls create_dir_all there), and an IO error at that point is unreachable by the application: it panics with 'Failed to setup app: Permission denied (os error 13)' at tauri-2.11.2/src/app.rs:1417, before Tine's setup hook runs. A user whose ~/.local/share is root-owned - the shape of the box this was found on, drwxr-xr-t root root - therefore got a hard crash with a backtrace and no actionable message, made more confusing by Tine's own desktop-identity step logging the same Permission denied and explicitly treating it as NON-fatal one line earlier. data_home::ensure_usable now probes the directory before anything resolves it (create_dir_all is not the question: it succeeds on an existing directory nobody may write) and, when it is unusable, points XDG_DATA_HOME at the first writable fallback for that launch - ~/.tine-data, then $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/tine-data, then a uid-namespaced temp dir - so settings, session and the WebView store live somewhere real. XDG_DATA_HOME is the one lever that redirects Tauri's path resolver, WebKitGTK's website-data manager and Tine's own settings together. The frontend toasts once, stickily, naming the directory, because a silent relocation is its own defect. If nothing at all is writable the app prints one actionable sentence and exits 1 rather than panicking. Verified on the built binary: unwritable base -> app stays up, ~/.tine-data/page.tine.Tine populated with tine-settings.json and the WebKit store, nothing written to the read-only base; ordinary writable base -> no relocation diagnostic at all and no probe residue.

entries.title: A graph whose watch() failed stays blind to external changes while another graph is watched
entries.notes: Direct Files data-safety audit 2026-08-09, finding 16, landed in its REACHABLE form only. The audit claimed an inotify watch() failure leaves the watcher permanently blind with no poll fallback; that is not what the code does. A failed root is never inserted into `watched` and is retried on the next cycle, and when EVERY root fails `watched` is empty, which takes the else branch and its bounded <=3 s recv_timeout - a working recovery loop. The reachable case is mixed: with two graphs open, the inotify branch blocks on rx.recv() until an event arrives from a root that IS watched, so a root the kernel refused is retried only when some other graph happens to change. inotify limits are per-user (fs.inotify.max_user_watches), so opening a second large graph is exactly how one root fails while the other is healthy, and on a quiet healthy graph the failing one stays invisible indefinitely. inotify_cycle_wait now bounds the wait to UNWATCHED_ROOT_RETRY (3 s, matching the poll branch ceiling) whenever a desired root is unwatched, and never delays a sooner scheduled retry. Coverage gaps stated in the tests themselves: they pin the wait policy, not a real kernel watch() failure (which needs privileges unavailable here) and not the call-site wiring, and they are a specification rather than fail-before evidence because the function is new.

entries.title: Every typing lull shipped the whole reference-name inventory across IPC
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F7. The frontend's reference-name resource is keyed on dataRev, which a save bumps ~700 ms after every typing lull, so referenced_page_names ran and its result crossed IPC on every pause in typing: measured 15-23 ms and about 5,000 names at 5,225 files, with the JSON parse landing on the UI thread. The answer almost never changes, because typing inside a block rarely adds or removes a [[link]]. referenced_page_names now takes the digest of the set the caller already holds and omits the payload when it still matches, so the ordinary case is an integer. The digest is a commutative fold with the length mixed in: the memo's order comes from a HashMap, so a sequence-dependent hash would report a change on every rebuild and the gate would save nothing. NOT fixed here: the whole-graph recompute itself still runs once per cache generation, because computing the digest needs the names; making it incremental needs per-name reference counts in cache_upsert/cache_remove and is a separate packet. The frontend test pins the dangerous reading of an omitted payload - treating it as an empty set would erase every reference-only page from autocomplete and the namespace tree - and that the digest is actually presented back.

entries.title: Every save case-folded and NFC-normalised every filename in the target's directory
entries.notes: Direct Files performance audit 2026-08-09, finding F6. validate_graph_text_portable_aliases_path_local enumerates each path component's directory looking for case/NFC aliases of the target, and built a PortablePathKey for EVERY entry - a String allocation plus NFD -> default case fold -> NFC per filename. The audit's controlled experiment held graph size constant and varied only layout: 4.87 ms/save with 4,000 pages in one directory versus 0.70 ms with 40 per subdirectory, i.e. 6.9x on layout alone, growing without bound on the one directory that only ever grows (journals/) and running inside the identity-mutation lock. PortablePathKey::graph_text_components_match answers the same question without building either key when both sides are ASCII, where NFD/NFC are the identity and default case folding is exactly ASCII lowercasing. Controlled A/B on this box, same graph and build, 4,000 pages in one directory, 60 saves x 3 runs: 2.54-2.67 ms median before, 1.39-1.41 ms after (~1.8x). The both-sides-ASCII guard is load-bearing rather than redundant: folding can PRODUCE ASCII from non-ASCII (U+212A KELVIN SIGN folds to k, U+FB01 to fi), so a non-ASCII name can legitimately collide with an ASCII one and must still take the full fold. This is an identity boundary whose failure mode is admitting a collision, so the test asserts agreement with the full fold over every ordered pair of a name set that includes NFC/NFD twins, the sharp s, Cyrillic, and both fold-to-ASCII traps. Residual NOT fixed: the directory enumeration is still O(entries); removing that needs the maintained admission index to become the authority for this check, which is a data-safety boundary change and its own packet.

entries.title: A Safe reopen confirms a closed-interval rename before a negative page lookup offers a new draft
entries.notes: Fail-before at 3158cbae: after a Safe handoff, a filesystem rename during the closed interval made the first editor name lookup return NewPage. The startup census correctly found the new file but only staged the old path absence; its post-drain scan is intentionally not independent, so it could acknowledge the queue without admitting the replacement. A negative read now requests one bounded rescan epoch before returning Missing/NewPage. The regression proves the single replacement batch removes the old name and exact path, exposes the new name and exact path with its source content, and leaves no watcher work pending.

entries.title: A duplicated "Keep mine" spent authority minted for a newer winner nobody was shown
entries.notes: GH #254 increment 2, adversarial implementation verification finding 1 (CRITICAL) and the reachable half of finding 2. A force request named its authority only by path plus loaded revision, so consume_conflict_authority could only check SELF-consistency - that the live token is the newest - never that the user had seen it. Reachable data loss with no malicious writer: an external editor or sync client publishes B after the banner showed A; two force requests are in flight under that one banner (the button is not disabled while its request is pending) and the per-page save queue serializes them; the first correctly refuses B and, being a coherent observation, mints fresh authority FOR B; the second, issued before B existed, consumed it and overwrote B. A conflict error now carries the observation epoch it minted at, direct_save_error_message emits it as 'conflict:<n>', the frontend stores it with the banner and echoes it back on force, and consumption requires the presented epoch to equal the live token's. Found while fixing: checking ownership AFTER taking would let one stray duplicate click disarm the banner permanently, so a mis-addressed override is now refused WITHOUT spending the live token - covered by its own test. A force that can name no observation is refused at the command boundary rather than allowed to consume whatever is current. Necessity: all three new core tests fail against the pre-fix check.

entries.title: Managed page and journal deletion preserves the exact accepted projection bytes in typed trash before accepting the tombstone
entries.notes: Accepted managed-storage safety repair, 2026-08-10. An ordinary managed delete derives its exact page ID, accepted path, kind and actor source bytes from one actor turn; durably publishes those exact bytes to logseq/.tine-trash/pages or journals with no overwrite; then re-proves the same actor source, page identity and accepted-frontier root before authoring exactly one DeletePage. H4 adds a retained capability walk from the projection root through logseq, .tine-trash and the typed kind directory: every component is created with ensure_directory_nofollow and reopened with open_dir_nofollow, then tine-storage v0.1.1 publish_immutable_exact publishes or exact-verifies the leaf. On Windows the storage contract is its certified, validated-directory ceiling; it does not claim undocumented power-loss directory fsync. Focused Rust tests cover managed application save followed by exact projected-byte recovery, imported page and journal CRLF/layout, original extension, idempotent unpinned retry, the fresh/malformed typed chain, and a publication failure after optional leaf creation: it refuses before a tombstone or frontier/author advance, leaves the source, and an exact retry converges. Frontend tests cover the bounded page-local quiescence barrier, in-flight second edit, an edit in the resolved-helper handoff, retained save/deferred drafts, and the explicit conflicted-delete path: no draft flush, backend actor invocation, removal only on success, and draft retention on failure. Source-proven fail-before: the prior ordinary DeletePage authored its semantic tombstone without any preservation/re-proof, and its frontend path performed only one dirty flush with no synchronous retirement recheck. Direct Files backend/trash semantics remain unchanged.
